newsitem.title: USA: U.S. truckers seen weathering rail merger fervor.
newsitem.headline: U.S. truckers seen weathering rail merger fervor.

text.p: The recent wave of rail mergers seems unlikely to shatter the dominance of trucking companies in transporting freight.

A Conrail link-up with either CSX Corp., which has put forth an $8.4 billion bid for the northeastern rail line, or with Norfolk Southern Corp., which announced a $9.0 billion counter-offer on Wednesday, could eventually siphon off some market share on longer-haul routes.
But U.S. truckers are unlikely to feel the heat from the railroads for several years, if at all, analysts say.

"I don't believe that (a merger) will have a significant effect on trucking," said Stephen Klein, analyst with Standard & Poor's. "It's not going to drop the rates for intermodal transport significantly enough that it would attract any more traffic."

"Truckers don't seem to be quaking in their boots," said another industry analyst, who requested anonymity. "Railroads have been trying to take revenue for a long time, and they are starting to make a little headway now, but ... people are not really sold on it."

In dollar terms, U.S. truckers carry about 10 times the amount of freight that rail moves, analysts say. While rail is typically the cheapest way to transort goods in the continental United States, truckers score high marks for on-time performance and overall efficiency.
"The railroads get you farther for your transport dollar," said Renee Johansen, who follows the trucking industry for Wheat First Butcher Singer.
"The question is, if you need it there with 99 percent reliability ... it needs to move by truck."
In announcing their merger plans, executives from both Conrail and CSX emphasized the potential for the new company to compete with truckers, especially along the densely-populated East Coast.
"The new company we are creating will be more competitive with trucks and other modes of transportation," Conrail Chairman David LeVan said in a statement.
"... We will provide our customers one point of contract, and eliminate the costs and delyas now layered over every step in the service porcess."
Fusing the two networks' operations would provide a stiff challenge to truckers on the heavily-trafficked north-south Interstate 95 highway, the companies said.

Norfolk Southern did not hone in on the trucking industry when it formally announced its rival bid, but analysts saw little difference for truckers from either a Norfolk-Conrail or a CSX-Conrail marriage.

"I don't think that one is necessarily going to be superior over the other," said Wheat First's Johansen. "CSX comes closer along the (east) coast" than Norfolk Southern, but both Conrail suitors maintain large networks in the inland southeast, she added.

In either scenario, the combined railroad would be poised to improve service and cut transit time on the north-south corridor, and may slash prices on certain routes in an effort to draw business away from trucking companies.

Indeed, with the explosive growth of intermodal transport -- in which both rail and truck are used to carry freight to a final destination -- analysts said the railroads' increased efficiency might actually benefit trucking companies.

"Some of the biggest clients of the railroad companies are now trucking companies," said Professor Yossi Sheffi, director of the Center for Transportation Studies at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
"If the railroad will be able to offer faster and more reliable intermodal service, this will help trucking."

Analysts pointed out that truckers had already faced down a similar threat in the West, when Burlington Northern acquired Sante Fe railroad in a $4 million deal, and Union Pacific Corp. swallowed up Southern Pacific Rail Corp. to form the largest rail network in the country.

"(Those mergers) took place over a year ago and you don't see a big pick-up in their intermodal traffic," said S&P's Klein. Instead, he said, railroads have continued to lose market share to truckers in the last year and a half.
But some industry watchers say it may simply be too early to weigh the effects of the earlier rail mergers.
"It will take several years to start seeing better schedules and faster trends," said Sheffi.
While the merged railroads have yet to offer substantially improved schedules, Sheffi said, those changes would take years to implement.
Truckers, for their part, have so far dowplayed the threat to their business.
"Seventy-five percent of the communities in this country rely exclusively on trucking for their freight service," said James Lewis, spokesman for the American Trucking Associations, a trade group.
"Unless somebody is planning on laying a lot more rail, we don't expect that to change significantly."
